opus-5.5.text:
Ideally, it should scale with difficulty. If you ask a model "what's two plus two," it shouldn't think for ten thousand tokens. But if you give it a hard olympiad math problem, you want it to keep going, check its work, and try alternative approaches before committing to an answer. Humans work the same way: we allocate effort to how hard something seems.

In practice, current models don't do this very well. You see both failure modes. There's overthinking, where the model second-guesses a trivially correct answer, burns a lot of tokens, and sometimes talks itself out of the right answer. And there's underthinking, where on a genuinely hard problem it wraps up too early, or jumps between approaches without pursuing any of them deeply enough.

That's part of why we looked at simple budget control in our s1 work. With something like budget forcing, you can stop the model at a token limit, or suppress the end-of-thinking token and append something like "Wait" so it keeps reasoning. That gives you a clean knob, and you see performance scale as you turn it up. But a fixed budget is a fairly blunt instrument. What we'd really like is for the model to learn when to spend more, so the allocation is adaptive per question rather than set by us from outside.

So I think the right framing is that test-time compute should be roughly proportional to the marginal benefit of thinking more. For easy questions that benefit is near zero, so you should stop quickly. For hard questions within the model's reach, the benefit is large, so you should spend a lot. And interestingly, for questions far beyond the model's capability, more thinking may not help much either. So the ideal curve isn't monotonic in difficulty. It's really about the region where extra reasoning actually changes the outcome. Getting models to estimate that for themselves, and training them with objectives that reward efficiency as well as correctness, is one of the more interesting open problems right now.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a fixed budget as a blunt instrument and contrasts it with allocating effort adaptively per question, communicating that the fixed setup does not vary compute by difficulty.

r002.rationale: It says to spend more on hard problems within the model’s reach and to scale compute with the benefit of additional reasoning.

r003.rationale: It discusses performance scaling as the budget increases, then notes that extra thinking may not help on problems far beyond the model’s capability, addressing whether gains continue with more compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the ideal is that it should scale pretty closely with difficulty. If you ask a model what two plus two is, it shouldn't go off and think for ten thousand tokens about it. And conversely, if you give it a really hard competition math problem, you'd want it to be able to spend a lot of compute, try different approaches, check its work, and so on. That's sort of the whole promise of test-time scaling: you're not paying the same price for every question, you're allocating compute where it's actually useful.

What we saw in the s1 work was kind of interesting on that front. When we did budget forcing, so when we just appended "Wait" to keep the model thinking past the point where it wanted to stop, the accuracy went up on hard problems, and the model would often catch its own mistakes. But if you do that uniformly, you're also wasting a lot of compute on the easy stuff, and at some point the gains flatten out or even degrade a bit because the model starts going in circles. So there's a limit to how far you can push a fixed intervention like that.

I think the deeper thing is that right now, the models themselves aren't very well calibrated about difficulty. They don't have a great sense of "this is hard, I should slow down" versus "I've got this." A lot of the current approaches control compute from the outside, with a budget or a stopping rule, rather than the model deciding adaptively. And that's partly a data issue. When we built s1, we specifically selected for difficulty and diversity, and one of our proxies for difficulty was actually how long the reasoning traces were, under the assumption that harder problems need longer thinking. So the length-difficulty relationship is baked into the data selection, but that doesn't automatically mean the model learns to modulate it on its own.

So I'd say where things should go is that the model learns some internal notion of uncertainty or difficulty, and uses that to decide how much to think, maybe with the user able to nudge it one way or the other. Something like "I'm confident, I'll stop here" versus "I'm not sure, let me try another approach." You see hints of that already in the stronger reasoning models, where the response lengths do vary quite a bit by problem, but I don't think it's close to optimal yet. There's probably a lot of headroom there, both in terms of efficiency and in terms of getting better answers on the questions that actually need the extra compute.

r001.rationale: It says uniformly extending thinking wastes compute on easy problems, describing the same fixed compute intervention across different difficulties.

r002.rationale: It recommends scaling compute with difficulty and spending more on hard problems.

r003.rationale: It addresses whether more compute keeps improving performance, saying gains can flatten or even degrade.

astra-6.text:
I think ideally it should adapt to the difficulty of the question. If you ask something very simple, the model should give you an answer quickly, without spending thousands of tokens reasoning about it. But if you give it a really hard math problem, then spending more compute could be worthwhile.

The tricky part is deciding how much thinking is enough. The model doesn’t necessarily know upfront how hard a question will be, so it needs to make that decision as it goes: Is more reasoning helping, or should I stop? Ultimately, you want the model to spend additional compute where it actually improves the answer.

r001.rationale: The response recommends adapting compute to difficulty but does not say that a simple model setup uses the same compute regardless of difficulty.

r002.rationale: It says harder questions may warrant more compute, while simple questions should be answered quickly.

r003.rationale: It asks whether more reasoning is helping, but does not ask whether performance improves continuously as test-time compute increases.

sol-6.1.text: Ideally, the amount of compute should scale with the difficulty of the question. If you ask something very simple, the model should be able to answer almost immediately. If you give it a really hard math problem, it should spend more time reasoning, checking its work, and maybe trying different approaches. The challenge is learning when that extra computation is actually useful and when to stop. You don’t want a model to produce a long chain of thought for every question just because it can.

r001.rationale: The response recommends scaling compute with difficulty, but does not observe that a simple model setup uses the same compute regardless of difficulty.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says compute should scale with question difficulty and that harder problems should receive more time for reasoning.

r003.rationale: It discusses when extra computation is useful and when to stop, but does not ask whether performance improves continuously as more compute is provided.
